analysis.one_liner: Eliminates all copays and deductibles for insulin and injection supplies under Medicare and Medicaid.
analysis.headline: The bill to end insulin copays for Medicare and Medicaid patients drew 63 cosponsors but never got a hearing or a vote in two years.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have removed all deductibles, copays, and coinsurance for insulin and insulin-injection supplies for people on Medicare's prescription drug benefit and on Medicaid. It was referred to two House committees in January 2019 and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare Part D enrollees and Medicaid beneficiaries who use insulin would pay no deductible, copayment, or coinsurance for insulin or the supplies used to inject it, starting January 1, 2020 [S2][S3]. This group is disproportionately older, disabled, and low-income people for whom even modest copays can mean rationing a drug they cannot safely skip.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare and Medicaid patients with diabetes

how_it_helps.text: Medicare Part D enrollees would pay no deductible, copayment, coinsurance, or other cost-sharing for insulin or for the medical supplies used to inject it, starting January 1, 2020.
Medicaid beneficiaries would be exempt from premiums and cost-sharing for insulin and associated supplies under standard plans and under alternative benefit plans.
For people who rely on insulin daily, the bill removed the out-of-pocket barrier most directly linked to insulin rationing, a practice that can be fatal.

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the cost of insulin and supplies now paid by patients through deductibles and copays would have shifted to the federal Medicare program and to Medicaid, split between the federal government and the states. Insurers administering Medicare Part D plans would lose the copay and deductible revenue but would be made whole through higher federal plan payments. Drug makers would face no direct cost, since the bill did not cap insulin prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers and state Medicaid budgets

drawbacks.text: The bill addressed only what patients pay at the counter, not the underlying insulin prices, so public programs and taxpayers would have absorbed the full cost of a drug whose list prices had climbed for years without any downward pressure on the manufacturers.

Eliminating cost-sharing for an entire class of drugs adds new federal spending to Medicare and new costs to state Medicaid budgets, which share Medicaid financing; some states would have needed to pass legislation to comply, and the bill allowed them to delay until after their next legislative session.
The benefit was limited to public insurance programs, leaving the millions of people with private or no insurance, who faced the same insulin prices, without help.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The patient benefit was real and targeted: people on Medicare and Medicaid who need insulin every day would have stopped paying anything out of pocket for the drug and its supplies. The cost was a genuine increase in federal and state spending, and the bill's design had a real weakness — it paid insulin's high prices rather than lowering them, which is why even supporters framed similar proposals as a first step rather than a fix. The narrower scope also excluded people with private or no insurance. On balance, for the population it covered, the health benefit of removing cost barriers to a life-sustaining drug outweighed the added public cost, but the bill never got far enough for that trade-off to be debated on the floor.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in two House committees and their Health subcommittees for two years without ever getting a hearing or a vote, and it died when the Congress ended January 3, 2021.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 9, 2019, by Rep. Bobby Rush along with 34 original cosponsors, all Democrats.
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, and both referrals were then sent to Health subcommittees by late January and early March 2019.
No further action of any kind — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — was recorded for the rest of the two-year Congress.
The bill attracted 63 cosponsors by the end, all of them Democrats, and none of the committee or subcommittee action advanced it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare drug plans and insulin manufacturers kept the existing payment structure untouched: patients continued to pay cost-sharing out of pocket, and no new federal mandate reshaped the market. Taxpayers were spared the added federal and state spending the bill would have required.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers and Medicare drug plans

sides.party_line_note: All 64 initial supporters, including the sponsor and 63 cosponsors, were House Democrats, and no roll-call vote ever took place, so the bill never got past the committee stage where its fate was decided.

industries.note: The bill would not have cut insulin prices; it would have used public money to cover what patients pay at the pharmacy, so manufacturers' revenue stream stayed intact while their products became more accessible. Their pricing power over a drug people cannot live without is what made cost-sharing unaffordable in the first place.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D insurers and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: Part D plans would have lost copay and deductible revenue on insulin, but federal payments to plans would have risen to cover the eliminated cost-sharing, so the plans' overall economics were largely protected.

States would have been required to drop cost-sharing for insulin in Medicaid, with federal matching funds covering their share; the bill included a delay for states needing legislation, acknowledging the fiscal burden. It also locked in Medicaid's role as a guaranteed payer for insulin.
